label: text
text: Lord Russell of Killowen; Sir Frank Lockwood, K.O., Solicitor-General; Lord Burnham; Sir Charles Mathews, Director of Public Prosecutions; Sir John Hare; Sir Frank Burnand, editor of "Punch"; Sir John Tenniel, the cartoonist; Linley Sambourne, the artist; Rudolph Lehmann, and Mr. Furness.

label: text
text: The club was named by Sir Frank Burnand after "the two knights of the road, of course," John Gilpin and Dick Turpin, and members rode out of town each Sunday possible to lunch in some attractive place near London.

label: text
text: Mr. Burniss reveals in this book "a little mystery that puzzled the Pressmen of the time, and was known to very few members of the Garrick." At a critical period, "a short" while before the Balfour Government died of ennui," the Turner Councils within the Cabinet Council were held in the strangers' room of the Garrick Club. Nobody knew where the discussions took place, and so little known was Balfour at the club that his presence there passed unnoticed.

label: text
text:
The story of a sedate housekeeper who became a "bookie" is told by Mr. Furniss. A doctor in a provincial town died and left his house to his faithful housekeeper, so that she might take in lodgers.
But the doctor had been an ardent sportsman and keen racing man, and the quiet, uncommunicative housekeeper had learned more than her employer would ever have believed. After his death she used her knowledge to set up to business as a bookmaker, and in time built up a prosperous concern.

label: text
text: Mr. Furniss died as this, the last book he wrote, was passing through the press.

Carriso Gorge, one of the most desolately beautiful spots in the wild, fastness of the Mexican border, was the location Clarence G. Badger selected for filming exterior scenes for the Goldwyn picture, "Red Lights" which is showing at the World Theatre for the last time to-day. The story was adapted to the screen by Carey Wilson from the stage play, "The Rear Car."
123d Field Artillery band gave its first dance in 1911. Marie Prevost and Alice Lake were the popular belles of the evening. The mayor and sheriff centred their attentions on the two actresses.

label: text
text:
A special train of ten coaches, carrying a radio, an airplane, a five piece orchestra and a special car on which was mounted an electric generator left Los Angeles for the border with seventy-five members of the company including carpenters, electricians, property men, cameramen, extras, mechanics and technical men. Two immigration officers accompanied the party as representatives of the United States Government, for the greater portion of the railroad runs through Mexico. The little town of Jacumba Hot Springs was the destination of the Goldwyn special. With the arrival of the Goldwyn company the citizens of the town hailed a new era of prosperity. There had not been much excitement since the Mexican revolution, when Uncle Sam's soldiers camped about the town.
The few little dilapidated shacks and stores with sand drifted around the doorways did not present a very lively appearance to the movie crew. A company of gypsies had encamped just off the main street. Several fat, black Mexicans with stuffed black beards dozed on the steps of the pool hall. A limp cigarette dangled from the fat cheek of one of the idlers. Johnnie Walker slapped him on the back the cigarette dropped. He did not open his eyes but moved one foot to a more comfortable position. For five weeks the "Red Lights" company lived in their train side tracked at this little village.
The town was enlivened Saturday nights with a dance on the floor above the pool hall. The orchestra, which accompanied the "Red Lights" company, played the latest jazz strains and was voted the best orchestra that had appeared in the town since the

label: text
text: Several thrilling and laughable incidents marked the visit of the movie troupe.

label: text
text: One of these was provided, by Raymond Griffith. Along the route taken by the train are seventeen tunnels. The country is wild and infested with mountain lions and bobcats. Griffith was walking alone through one of these tunnels with a.32 automatic in his hand. A large boulder dropped with a thud from the top of the tunnel. In the black darkness of the tunnel this was very perturbing, to say the least. Griffith in his terror opened fire with his pistol, and emptied it in the direction of the rock which he had mistaken for a wildcat. Other members of the company rushed into the tunnel and found Ray sitting on the rock wiping his brow.

label: text
text:
Not being able to cash cheques, the actors were forced to beg credit at the stores. Many left town without their watches or other jewellery. When they arrived home they mailed money to pay their bills, and received their valuables in the next mail.
Clarence G. Badger worked night and day directing the railroad scenes for the picture. A special developing room aided the cameramen in making their tests. Some of the most successful and unusual night scenes were taken on the train.

label: text

All of which is recalled by a motion picture on view at the World Theatre to-morrow. It is William Fox's super special production, "The Last Trail," adapted from the novel of that name by the famous Zane Grey. Toward the close of the story a huge reservoir dam in the mountains is broken by dynamite explosion—the work of the Villian—and the liberated waters sweep down upon a village miles away.
To create this startling incident, which constitutes the big climax of the Fox picture, the director, Emmett J. Flynn, under took a singularly formidable task. He built the village in California valley. He constructed a big.com.
create dam high up in the hills. It was a costly enterprise, involving much valuable time and high-priced labour. But that the end justified the means will not be denied by anyone who witnesses the explosion and later views the village inhabitants fleeing to the hills, and the place destroyed.

label: text
text: Here is a thrill—or series of thrills—genuinely worth while in heart-reaching film entertainment. Director Flynn, by the way, has made a goodly number of Fox successes, but achieved special fame with the great Fox production, based on Mark Twain's masterpiece of satire, "A Conecticut Yankees in King Arthur's Court"—a picture that Joited New York into unusual enthusiasm and had a prolonged run of many months on Broadway before starting on its triumphant tour of the country.
